hook: The trick every gamer aged 8 to 10 should know
book_line: One piece is never just one piece. A few minutes, on the sofa.
thumb_title: One piece is never just one piece

ask1: Which three pieces did DiGi join up, and what did they make?
Older child: why is it cleverer to ask for three pieces in three places than all three at once?
ask2: Grown up, say these one at a time. Piece, or not a piece?
my favourite dinner · the name of our street · my football team · the day I was born
Slip a wrong one in on purpose.

child.text: Hello, you two. Yes, both of you, grown up as well. And Bloop, who has lost a jigsaw piece again.
By the end of this, you'll spot a trick that works on grown ups every day.
Three slow breaths, out longer than in. Breathe in for four. And out for six. Once more. This is a spotting job, and a fast brain walks straight past small things.
Remember the shield? Your name, where you live, your school, your photos, all kept behind it. Tonight, things are asking to come out.
Today's word is jigsaw. Small pieces that join up into a picture. And tonight, the picture is you.
Here's how it works. Monday. A game ends, and a box pops up: put your real name on the leaderboard. So you do.
Tuesday. A quiz. What animal are you? Pop in your birthday. Otter.
Wednesday. Someone in your team chat, nice to you for weeks, asks: which school do you go to? My cousin might be there. And you nearly answer, because it would feel rude not to.
Three little things, and not one of them felt like anything. Now watch them join.
Your name. Your birthday. Your school. That's enough to answer the little questions when someone taps forgot my password on your account. Somebody walking in through the front door.
Here's the bit to keep. Nobody asks for all three at once. You'd spot it straight away.

So it comes one piece at a time, on different days, and every piece feels like nothing. That isn't you missing something. That's the trick, working as it was built. And a trick you can see has stopped working.
Pause me here. Grown up, ask the question on the screen. I'll wait.

So how do you catch a piece? Three questions. Could this help somebody find me? Get into something of mine? Pretend to be me? If even one answer is yes, it's a piece. And pieces stay on your side of the screen.
Six things are always a yes, so you don't even need the test. Full name. School. Address. Phone number. Passwords. Any photo that shows where you live or learn.
Sometimes they do have to go in somewhere, like a school account. That's fine, because a grown up is doing it with you. On your own, they stay out.

A piece hardly ever looks like a question. It comes wrapped in something good. Free coins. A fun quiz. Somebody being really friendly. When something lovely turns up with a box underneath, that's your moment.
And there's one move to know by name. Someone from a game says: let's chat somewhere else. Or: don't tell anyone.
That's always a check with your grown up moment. Every time. Even if they've been lovely.

You're not being rude, and you're not deciding alone. In a chat you can say: nah, not that one, what's your best score? A box, you just shut. Then you mention it to your grown up. That's checking, not telling on anyone.
Pause me again. Grown up, say a few things out loud, one at a time. Piece, or not a piece?

child.word: One piece is never just one piece!
child.text: Out loud, both of you. Grown up first. One piece is never just one piece!

child.word: One piece is never just one piece!
child.text: Again, together. One piece is never just one piece!

child.word: One piece is never just one piece!
child.text: Last one, properly loud. One piece is never just one piece!
Tonight, play Five Pieces. Your grown up asks you five friendly questions. Some are pieces, some are just nice. A point for every piece you catch.
Then swap, and see if you can catch them out. Grown ups, let yourself get caught. It's the best bit.
One last thing, and it matters most. If you're thinking, I've already put some of that in somewhere, then good. Go and tell a grown up you trust. Tonight, or next week.
Usually that's the person sitting next to you. A teacher counts. A nan or an auntie counts. And Childline is free, on oh eight hundred, eleven eleven, any time.
child.cap: Usually that's the person sitting next to you. A teacher counts. A nan or an auntie counts. And Childline is free, on 0800 1111, any time.

child.text: Nothing is ruined. Some of it you change, some you take down. And you will never, ever be in trouble for telling.
Oh, Bloop. There it was. One piece is never just one piece.
Goodbye from Didgee. See you next time.

parent.text: More than half of children who game online sometimes play with people they've never met.
parent.cap: More than half of children who game online sometimes play with people they've never met. (Ofcom, Growing Up Gaming, October 2026)

parent.big: The game is where it starts. The private app is where it happens.
parent.text: Most of those people are other children. The risk is one move.
Then someone friendly says: let's chat somewhere else. And once chat leaves the game, nobody is moderating it.
parent.cap: Then someone friendly says: let's chat somewhere else. Once chat leaves the game, "no one is moderating it" (CEOP).

parent.big: If anyone asks you to move to another app, come and tell me. You won't lose the game for telling me.
parent.text: So make one promise tonight, before anything happens. If anyone asks you to move to another app, come and tell me. You won't lose the game for telling me.
Their film teaches the other half: private details get collected one small piece at a time, and how to spot it.
It's a few minutes on the sofa. In Guided Childhood, you can book a time to watch it together.
